individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: This paper presents ChartGalaxy, a large-scale dataset of infographic charts built by collecting 61,833 real charts and programmatically generating 1,701,356 synthetic charts from 75 chart types, 440 variations, and 68 layout templates extracted from real designs. The dataset pairs each chart with tabular data and is evaluated in three applications: instruction-tuning LVLMs for infographic chart understanding, benchmarking D3.js code generation, and example-based infographic chart generation. Results show gains over base models, a performance ranking of 17 LVLMs, and user-study improvements over GPT-Image-1.
Strengths: The dataset addresses a real gap: existing chart datasets focus on plain charts, while this one targets infographic charts with rich text-image-layout structure. The inductive process of extracting chart types, variations, and layout templates from real infographics and then synthesizing at scale is a thoughtful approach.

The three evaluations demonstrate the resource's utility: fine-tuning on ChartGalaxy improves both InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL on public benchmarks, the code-generation benchmark provides a reproducible comparison of 17 LVLMs, and the example-based generation method outperforms GPT-Image-1 in a user study.

The data collection pays attention to ethics and reproducibility: sources are limited to research-permitted and CC-licensed charts, URLs are released instead of images, the pipeline is described in detail, and the user study received IRB approval.
Weaknesses: The evaluation of understanding is limited: only two LVLMs are fine-tuned; the held-out evaluation set is synthetic and shares the same generative process as training data, so the substantial gains there may reflect distribution overlap. No human evaluation of answer correctness is reported, and no comparison to training on existing chart datasets is provided.

The code-generation benchmark uses only 500 synthetic charts from the same pipeline; this may not represent the difficulty of generating arbitrary real-world infographics. The high-level score is produced by GPT-4o without validation against human raters, and the low-level metric may not capture semantic quality.

The example-based generation method is essentially a template-filling system rather than a generative model, and the user study is small (16 experts, 30 pairs) and compares only against GPT-Image-1, which is not designed for data-accurate chart generation. Thus, the claimed superiority may be expected and does not demonstrate broad creative-generation capability.

The real-chart table extraction relies on LVLM agreement and human verification for only a fraction of inconsistencies; no inter-annotator agreement or error analysis is reported, so the reliability of the 61,833 real chart-table pairs is not established.

The synthetic charts may still have limited semantic coherence between text and visuals because titles are generated by LLMs and images are retrieved via embedding similarity; the paper does not analyze failure cases or visual quality of the generated synthetic corpus as a whole.
Questions: How do the fine-tuning improvements on public benchmarks change if the model is trained only on a 10% random subset of the instruction data, and does the gain plateau? This would help establish data efficiency.
Are the 500 code-generation charts balanced across all 75 chart types and 68 templates, and how do the benchmark scores correlate with human judgments of visual similarity?
What is the accuracy of the LVLM-based table extraction on real infographic charts when compared against a human-annotated gold set beyond the 200 exact-match review?
Does fine-tuning on the synthetic-only portion help or hurt on real-world infographic charts compared to fine-tuning on real-only data, and why is the effect larger on the synthetic eval set?
How often does the layout optimizer violate the minimum-distance constraint or produce charts that are hard to read, and is ink ratio a good proxy for quality?
Limitations: The dataset is limited to single-chart infographics; multi-chart infographic narratives are not covered.
Synthetic charts are generated from a fixed set of hand-defined templates and may not capture the full range of human design creativity or unusual layouts.
Real chart data is primarily in English and from sources biased toward North America and Europe, limiting global representativeness.
The automatic extraction of tables from real charts may introduce undetected errors, affecting downstream supervision.
The code-generation benchmark targets D3.js only and synthetic charts, so it may not generalize to other libraries or real-world chart images.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper introduces ChartGalaxy, a million-scale dataset of infographic charts (61,833 real and 1,701,356 synthetic) paired with tabular data, constructed by extracting 75 chart types, 440 variations, and 68 layout templates from real infographics and programmatically generating synthetic charts. It validates the dataset through three applications: fine-tuning LVLMs for infographic chart understanding improves performance on public benchmarks and a human-verified evaluation set; a benchmark for D3.js code generation across 17 LVLMs; and an example-based generation method that outperforms GPT-Image-1 in an expert user study.
Strengths: Large-scale, diverse dataset (1.7M synthetic + 61k real) with tabular data alignment, addressing a gap in infographic chart understanding/generation.
Inductive pipeline that extracts 75 chart types, 440 variations, and 68 layout templates from real designs, with human-in-the-loop detection model expansion, enabling systematic synthetic generation.

Demonstrates clear utility: fine-tuning LVLMs improves understanding on public benchmarks and their eval set; comprehensive code generation benchmark across 17 LVLMs; example-based generation outperforms GPT-Image-1 in expert study.
Thorough appendices provide extensive details on chart types, layout templates, prompts, ablations, and user study, supporting reproducibility.
Weaknesses: The evaluation set for understanding is sampled from ChartGalaxy synthetic charts, so reported gains may be inflated due to distribution overlap; no comparison with fine-tuning on existing chart instruction datasets.
The code generation benchmark only includes 500 synthetic charts; generalization to real infographic charts is untested.
The example-based generation method is only briefly described, and the user study compares only against GPT-Image-1 with 16 experts, limiting the strength of the claim.

Synthetic chart generation is limited to 68 templates and predefined chart variations; may not capture full diversity of real-world infographics, despite a 97.62% coverage measure that only quantifies coverage, not distribution alignment.
Potential closed loop in layout template extraction: the detection model is trained on synthetic charts generated from initial templates, which may bias discovery of novel layouts.
The real chart tabular data extraction relies heavily on LVLMs; the accuracy is only partially human-verified.
Questions: Were the 2,176 charts in the independent evaluation set selected to be representative of the full dataset, and is this set available for public use?
How does fine-tuning on ChartGalaxy compare with fine-tuning on other chart instruction datasets (e.g., ChartAssistant, ChartInstruct) when evaluated on InfographicVQA and ChartQAPro?
Could the authors provide quantitative evaluation of the layout detection model's accuracy, and how does the closed-loop training affect template diversity?
Why was the code generation benchmark limited to synthetic charts? Could real charts with manually reconstructed code be included to test generalization?
In the user study, what was the inter-rater reliability (e.g., Fleiss' kappa) among the 16 experts?
How are the licenses of icons and images from Noun Project/Flaticon compatible with redistribution of the derived synthetic charts?
Limitations: Single-chart infographics only; no multi-chart narratives.
Synthetic charts may be less diverse than real infographics, and the evaluation does not test real-world distribution directly.
Geographic/domain coverage is skewed towards North America/Europe and English language.
Real chart table extraction is automatic with LVLM verification, so residual errors may exist.
The code generation benchmark only covers D3.js and synthetic charts.
The example-based generation method has limited detail and evaluation scope.
Potential licensing and intellectual property issues for images and data sources.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: This paper introduces ChartGalaxy, a million-scale dataset for infographic chart understanding and generation, containing 61,833 real and 1,701,356 synthetic infographic charts. Real charts are collected from licensed websites and search engines, while synthetic charts are programmatically generated using 75 chart types, 440 chart variations, and 68 layout templates extracted from real designs via a human-in-the-loop pipeline. Each chart is paired with tabular data. The paper demonstrates three applications: fine-tuning LVLMs for infographic chart VQA, benchmarking LVLM code generation for infographic charts with 17 models, and an example-based infographic chart generation method that outperforms GPT-Image-1 in a user study.
Strengths: The dataset fills a clear gap: existing chart datasets focus mostly on plain charts, while this work provides a large-scale, diverse collection of infographic charts with paired tabular data.

The synthetic generation pipeline is well-motivated and grounded in real designs through 75 chart types, 440 variations, and 68 layout templates, enabling scalable creation of visually diverse infographics.

Three applications are thoughtfully designed and demonstrate concrete utility: VQA fine-tuning improves both InternVL3-8B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B on public benchmarks; code generation is benchmarked across a broad set of 17 LVLMs; and a user study compares example-based generation against GPT-Image-1 with statistically significant gains.

The paper includes useful diversity analyses (geographic, domain, linguistic, and DreamSim feature-space coverage) and a detailed ethics statement covering licensing, IRB approval, and sensitive-content filtering.
The writing is clear and the experimental sections are generally reproducible in terms of model configurations, prompts, and evaluation metrics.
Weaknesses: The independent evaluation set for VQA is also synthetic and generated by the same pipeline, so the large gains (+26.87 and +23.85) may partly reflect in-distribution overfitting and may not fully transfer to real infographic charts; public benchmark gains are much smaller.

Real chart tabular data is extracted by LVLMs with only 200 exact-match samples manually reviewed; the accuracy of the 61,833 real tables is not rigorously estimated, which could affect both training and benchmark quality.

The code generation benchmark is limited to 500 synthetic charts, so it does not measure performance on real infographic charts, and the benchmark may favor models that have seen similar D3.js/template-based patterns.

The example-based generation comparison uses only GPT-Image-1 as the baseline and only 16 experts rating 30 triples; the prompt and setup may not be fully optimized for GPT-Image-1, and other state-of-the-art chart generation methods are not compared.

The dataset is dominated by synthetic charts (96.5%), and the paper does not provide human perceptual evaluation of how representative the synthetic charts are relative to real infographics beyond an automatic feature-coverage metric.
Synthetic content is English-only, and geographic/domain distributions skew toward North America and Europe, limiting multilingual and cultural diversity.
Questions: If the independent VQA evaluation set is generated by the same pipeline used for training data, how can we be confident that the large fine-tuning improvements generalize to real infographic charts? Could you evaluate on a held-out set of real infographic charts (beyond InfographicVQA and ChartQAPro)?

For the 61,833 real charts, what is the estimated table-extraction error rate, and how were the 13.4% manually corrected tables quality-checked? Does table noise materially affect the reported VQA gains?

The code generation benchmark contains only 500 synthetic charts. Why were real infographic charts not included, and would performance on a real-chart subset change the conclusions about model ranking?

In the example-based generation user study, how were the 30 reference charts chosen, and why was GPT-Image-1 the only comparison baseline? Would different prompts or other chart-generation systems alter the relative ranking?
The DreamSim coverage metric shows 97.62% overlap, but was there any human study validating that synthetic charts appear as realistic and diverse as real infographics?
What safeguards ensure that synthesized charts using icon sets like Icon645 (CC BY-NC-SA) remain compliant with license terms when the dataset is redistributed, especially for derived images?
Limitations: Real chart table extraction relies on LVLMs and may contain undetected errors, especially for visually complex infographics.
The VQA evaluation set is drawn from the same synthetic distribution as training, limiting evidence of generalization to real infographic charts.
The code generation benchmark is synthetic-only and relatively small (500 charts), so results may not fully reflect real-world chart-to-code generation.
The user study for example-based generation uses a single baseline model and a limited number of expert raters and examples.
The dataset focuses on single-chart infographics and does not address multi-chart narratives or complex inter-chart storytelling.
Synthetic data is English-only and the underlying sources skew toward North American/European topics, so linguistic and cultural coverage is uneven.
Potential licensing and redistribution concerns for derived images and real chart URLs are acknowledged but not fully resolved.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper introduces ChartGalaxy, a million-scale dataset of infographic charts comprising 61,833 real and 1,701,356 synthetic charts paired with tabular data. A pipeline extracts 75 chart types, 440 chart variations, and 68 layout templates from real designs, then programmatically generates synthetic charts with D3.js. The authors demonstrate utility through three applications: instruction tuning for visual question answering (VQA), a code generation benchmark, and example-based chart generation. Fine-tuning LVLMs on ChartGalaxy improves performance on InfographicVQA and ChartQAPro, a benchmark of 17 LVLMs shows gaps in infographic chart code generation, and a user study shows their example-based method outperforms GPT-Image-1 on fidelity, aesthetics, and creativity.
Strengths: Large-scale, diverse dataset filling a gap in infographic chart resources, with both real and synthetic examples and paired tabular data.
Inductive template extraction pipeline with human-in-the-loop and detection model expansion is novel and grounds synthetic data in real design patterns.
Rich taxonomy of 75 chart types, 440 variations, and 68 layout templates, with detailed appendices that provide useful resources for the community.

Demonstrates practical utility through three applications: consistent VQA improvements, a broad LVLM code-generation benchmark, and an example-based generation method that significantly outperforms GPT-Image-1 in a user study.
Ethical considerations are addressed, including source licenses, sensitive content filtering, and IRB approval for the user study.
Weaknesses: The internal VQA evaluation set is sampled from the same synthetic distribution as the training data, likely inflating gains; public benchmark improvements are modest and there is no comparison to fine-tuning on existing chart datasets.
Real data table extraction relies on LVLM agreement with limited manual verification (only 200 exact matches reviewed), so table quality for the 61K real charts may be noisy.
The code generation benchmark is restricted to synthetic charts, so it does not measure performance on real-world infographics, and no comparison is made to existing benchmarks like ChartMimic.

The example-based generation user study uses only 16 experts and 30 pairs, and compares against a single image-generation model; the template-based method is expected to be more faithful by design, and subjective metrics need further validation.
The synthetic dataset is generated from only 68 layout templates; despite the reported 97.62% DreamSim coverage, it may not capture the full diversity of real infographic layouts.
Reproducibility is hindered in the provided manuscript by redacted prompts, algorithm pseudocode, and dataset URLs, which prevents independent verification of several key steps.
Questions: How much of the VQA gain is attributable to ChartGalaxy's diversity compared to fine-tuning on existing chart datasets of similar size (e.g., ChartQA, ChartInstruct)? Please provide an ablation.
What is the accuracy of the automatically extracted data tables for real infographic charts? Have you evaluated on a larger human-annotated subset beyond the 200 samples?
Why is the code generation benchmark limited to synthetic charts? How would the 17 models perform on real infographic charts, and what are the main failure modes?
In the example-based generation method, how do you ensure that the retrieved/reference template is compatible with the user's data, and what happens when the template is not compatible?
Could you provide details of the SVG element matching algorithm and analyze how sensitive the low-level metrics are to matching errors? Have you validated the automated metrics with human evaluation?
Did you compare the synthetic distribution to real distributions beyond DreamSim coverage? Could the 68 templates be limiting in capturing multi-chart infographics or more complex real-world layouts?
Limitations: The dataset focuses on single-chart infographics; multi-chart narratives are not covered, as acknowledged by the authors.
Synthetic charts are generated from a finite set of templates and variations, which may introduce bias toward the collected sources (e.g., Statista, Visual Capitalist).
Real chart data tables are extracted automatically and may contain errors, affecting the reliability of the real subset.
The user study for example-based generation is small and subjective; results may not generalize.
Real charts are released only as URLs, which could break or become inaccessible over time.
The dataset is predominantly English-oriented, with limited multilingual coverage.

review.Summary: The paper introduces ChartGalaxy, a large-scale dataset for infographic chart understanding and generation, comprising 61,833 real infographic charts and 1,701,356 programmatically generated synthetic charts, each paired with tabular data. The construction pipeline identifies 75 chart types, 440 chart variations, and 68 layout templates from real designs, and uses them to synthesize diverse infographic charts with D3.js. The authors demonstrate utility through three applications: fine-tuning LVLMs for infographic chart VQA (improving InternVL3-8B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B on public benchmarks and a custom evaluation set), benchmarking chart-to-code generation across 17 LVLMs, and an example-based infographic chart generation method evaluated via a user study against GPT-Image-1.
Strengths: Large-scale resource: 1.7M+ synthetic and 61k real infographic charts with aligned tabular data, covering 75 chart types, 440 variations, and 68 layout templates.
The synthetic data pipeline is well-structured and grounded in real infographics via a human-in-the-loop template extraction process, enabling diverse programmatic generation beyond plain charts.

Three applications demonstrate practical utility: fine-tuning on ChartGalaxy yields consistent improvements on InfographicVQA and ChartQAPro; the code generation benchmark covers 17 LVLMs with fine-grained SVG-based metrics; and a user study shows higher fidelity, aesthetics, and creativity than GPT-Image-1.
The paper provides extensive documentation in appendices, including data licenses, table extraction pipeline, chart types/variations, templates, evaluation details, and ethics considerations.
Weaknesses: The VQA evaluation relies heavily on a self-constructed evaluation set sharing the same synthetic distribution as the training data; gains there (e.g., +60.49 on style detection) may partly reflect training-test homogeneity, and public-benchmark gains are more modest.

The code generation benchmark is restricted to synthetic charts; real infographic charts often contain photographic images and more complex text-visual interplay, so performance on this benchmark may not fully transfer to real-world infographics.

Data table extraction for real charts uses LVLMs with only a small manual verification subset (200 exact matches reviewed); errors in extracted tables could propagate into both real and synthetic data.

The example-based generation method is a fairly direct reuse of layout templates; the user study uses only 16 experts, 30 pairs, and a single baseline (GPT-Image-1), limiting the strength of the comparative claim.

Some reproducibility details are not fully available in the manuscript text (e.g., actual prompt contents, layout template diagrams, annotation guidelines), making reproduction dependent on the promised code/data release.
Questions: How was the 1,500-chart manual annotation sample selected, and what was the inter-annotator agreement for the initial 55 layout templates?
How was the independent VQA evaluation set human-verified? How many annotators were involved, and what quality-assurance process was used for the 4,975 question-answer pairs?
Why is the code generation benchmark limited to synthetic charts? Would the benchmark also be feasible for real charts, and how would model performance differ on real-world infographics?

What would happen if models were fine-tuned on a similarly sized sample of existing plain-chart instruction data (e.g., ChartAssistant or ChartQA-derived data) instead of ChartGalaxy? Is the observed improvement due to infographic-specific design, dataset scale, or question style?

Were the 120,000 synthetic charts used to train the detection model also included in the final dataset or evaluation sets? Are there near-duplicates or template-based overlaps between training and evaluation data that could inflate results?
How are the 68 layout templates distributed across the 1.7M synthetic charts? Is every template and variation represented, and could the popularity skew of certain templates reduce diversity?
Limitations: Real-chart table extraction via LVLMs may introduce errors; only a small subset was manually reviewed.
Synthetic charts are generated from a finite set of 68 layout templates and 440 chart variations, which may not capture the full long-tail diversity of real infographics.

The dataset is predominantly English (all synthetic charts and most real charts), with geographic and domain distributions skewed toward North America/Europe and certain topics such as public health and business.
Only single-chart infographics are included; multi-chart narratives and complex storytelling infographics are not addressed.
Fine-tuning on ChartGalaxy's synthetic QA data may cause overfitting to the synthetic style, as evidenced by large gains on the self-constructed evaluation set.
Potential negative societal impacts of generating infographics (e.g., misleading data presentation) are not discussed in the paper.

review.Summary: The paper introduces ChartGalaxy, a large-scale dataset of infographic charts consisting of 61,833 real charts and 1,701,356 programmatically generated synthetic charts, each paired with tabular data. The construction pipeline extracts 75 chart types, 440 chart variations, and 68 layout templates from real infographic designs via a human-in-the-loop approach, and uses them to synthesize diverse charts with D3.js. The dataset is evaluated in three applications: fine-tuning LVLMs for infographic chart VQA, benchmarking D3.js code generation across 17 LVLMs, and example-based infographic chart generation compared against GPT-Image-1 in a user study.
Strengths: Fills a clear gap in chart datasets by targeting infographic charts with rich text-image-layout structure, providing a large-scale resource of 61,833 real and 1,701,356 synthetic charts with aligned tabular data.

The inductive pipeline that extracts chart types, variations, and layout templates from real infographics and synthesizes at scale is well-motivated and grounded in real designs, with detailed appendices supporting reproducibility.

Demonstrates utility across three applications: fine-tuning on ChartGalaxy improves InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL on InfographicVQA and ChartQAPro; the code generation benchmark provides a broad comparison of 17 LVLMs with fine-grained metrics; and the example-based generation method outperforms GPT-Image-1 in an expert user study.
The paper addresses ethics and reproducibility through careful source licensing, sensitive-content filtering, IRB approval for the user study, and release of chart URLs rather than images.
The authors provide extensive documentation of chart types, variations, layout templates, prompts, ablations, and user study details.
Weaknesses: The independent VQA evaluation set is sampled from the same synthetic distribution as the training data, so the reported gains (e.g., +60.49 on style detection) may be inflated by distribution overlap; public benchmark gains are more modest, and no comparison is made with existing chart instruction datasets.
Real chart table extraction relies on LVLM agreement with only a small manual verification subset (200 exact-match samples), leaving the error rate of the 61,833 real chart-table pairs uncertain.

The code generation benchmark is limited to 500 synthetic charts generated from the same pipeline, so it may not represent arbitrary real-world infographics; the high-level score from GPT-4o is not validated against human raters, and the low-level SVG metric may miss semantic quality.

The example-based generation method is essentially a template-filling approach, and the user study uses only 16 experts and 30 pairs with a single baseline (GPT-Image-1), which may not be optimized for data-accurate chart generation; this limits the strength of the comparative claim.

Synthetic charts are limited to 68 layout templates and 440 variations, which may not capture the full long-tail diversity of real infographics; the paper does not provide human perceptual validation of realism beyond an automatic DreamSim coverage metric.

Reproducibility is partly hindered in the manuscript by redacted prompts, algorithm pseudocode, and dataset URLs, and the closed-loop training of the detection model on synthetic charts may bias template discovery.
The dataset is English-only, with geographic/domain skew toward North America and Europe, and it does not cover multi-chart infographic narratives.
Questions: How does fine-tuning on ChartGalaxy compare with fine-tuning on existing chart instruction datasets (e.g., ChartAssistant, ChartInstruct) of similar size when evaluated on InfographicVQA and ChartQAPro?
What is the estimated error rate of the LVLM-based table extraction on real infographic charts, and how were the 13.4% manually corrected tables quality-checked?
Why is the code generation benchmark limited to synthetic charts, and how would the 17 models perform on a real-chart subset with reconstructed code?
How were the 30 reference charts and 16 experts selected in the user study, and would different prompts or additional baselines change the relative ranking?

Were the 120,000 synthetic charts used to train the detection model also included in the final dataset or evaluation sets, and are there near-duplicates between training and evaluation data that could inflate results?
How are the 68 layout templates distributed across the 1.7M synthetic charts, and does the popularity skew of certain templates reduce diversity?
Limitations: The dataset covers only single-chart infographics; multi-chart narratives and complex storytelling infographics are not addressed.
Synthetic charts are generated from a finite set of templates and predefined variations, which may not capture the full creative diversity of human-designed infographics.
Automatic table extraction from real charts may introduce undetected errors, affecting both the real and synthetic portions of the dataset.
The dataset is predominantly English and geographically/domain-skewed toward North America/Europe, limiting global representativeness.
The code generation benchmark targets D3.js and synthetic charts only, so findings may not generalize to other libraries or real-world chart images.
Real charts are released as URLs that may become inaccessible over time.
Potential negative societal impacts of generating infographics, such as misleading data presentation, are not discussed.
